..
Issued at 231 AM CST Wed Nov 25 2026

08Z water vapor imagery showed a closed upper low spinning over SD 
and moving south along the MO river valley. A second shortwave was 
moving over the southern MS river valley. At the surface, obs placed 
the center of high pressure over the Upper Midwest with a surface 
ridge axis stretching into the southern plains. Based on the last 
several RAOBs from TOP, there was still an impressive sub-cloud dry 
layer. 

There are several time frames of interest in the forecast. The first 
is today with the closed upper low passing over northeast KS. Models 
show good mid level saturation with some disorganized mid level 
frontogenesis. Overall synoptic scale forcing is also limited with 
no real moisture advection ahead of the upper low. But there could 
be enough lift within the cloud for some flurries to develop this 
morning. The HRRR/RRFS kind of flip flop between showing some light 
reflectivity to no reflectivity across the forecast area. With the 
sub-cloud dry layer progged to persist through the morning, it looks 
difficult for any measurable precip to develop and have kept a 
mention of flurries in the forecast. 

Then for Thanksgiving, models have trended towards deepening the 
closed upper low as it enters the TN river valley. This is progged 
to wrap some mid level moisture back into northwestern MO and 
eastern KS Thursday morning. However there is no signal from the 
models of any forcing for vertical motion this far west. And none of 
the deterministic models have any QPF across the eastern parts of 
the forecast area. Looking at the ensemble data also supports the 
increasing moisture into a stable airmass. Ensembles show about a 10 
percent chance for a trace of precip in Douglas county tomorrow 
morning. The NBM had quite a gradient over the far eastern parts of 
the forecast area going from zero to categorical over the span of a 
county. Based on what I've seen this is much to aggressive in POPs. 
I still have some 20 to 30 percent POPs across the far eastern 
counties. If there ends up being some vertical motion for precip, 
amounts look to be around a hundredth of an inch with limited if 
any impacts to travel. 

The next opportunity for precipitation looks to come Saturday night 
and into Sunday morning. The 00Z ensembles are showing more support 
for the more amplified solution from the ECMWF with about three 
quarters of the ensembles with some kind of shortwave. This signal 
is also evident in the AIGEFS and HGEFS progs. Because of this 
confidence is increasing that we will see some precipitation with 
this wave. The big question is what form will the precip take. 
Ensembles and the NBM show very small chances for snow or other 
frozen precip Sunday morning with lows forecast to be in the middle 
30s for the most part. However the 00Z ECMWF and Canadian solutions 
have decent cold air advection developing late Saturday night with 
850MB temps dropping below zero during the overnight hours. This 
makes me wonder how much of the blend is affected by the less 
amplified and warmer GFS and its ensembles. In general think the 
trend towards a more amplified wave and higher precip chances is the 
right way to go. And I wouldn't be surprised if some light snow were 
to mix in on the back edge of the precip shield as temps fall Sunday 
morning. For now the NBM has all rain for the area. 

Another shortwave is progged to move through the central plains 
early next week. But surface ridging over the southern plains is 
progged to limit moisture availability with this wave. So the 
forecast keeps POPs at less than 10 percent. Occasional clouds and 
continued northerly winds are expected to keep temps below normal 
for today and Thanksgiving. Better return flow develops Friday and 
Saturday which should bump highs up into the 50s. By next week, 
ensembles want to develop a split flow pattern across North America 
with a more progressive pattern and less opportunities for cold air 
intrusions from the north. This is expected to keep more seasonal 
temps in place.
